AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?

26

9

Frontier models are improving design automation, but layouts, waveforms, and other semiconductor-specific data presents challenges that general-purpose AI has yet to fully overcome.

November 24th, 2026 -

By: Ann Mutschler

Key Takeaways:

Agentic AI could dramatically increase chip design productivity, but multiplying autonomous workloads will place unprecedented demands on EDA data management systems, compute resources, and network infrastructure.
Fragmented design data, inconsistent data quality, and strict IP security requirements are major obstacles to deploying AI at scale, making data governance, accessibility, and traceability increasingly critical.
Frontier AI models are becoming more capable of automating traditional EDA workflows, but achieving deeper optimization of chip layouts, waveforms, and other domain-specific data may require specialized models and hybrid AI architectures.

Experts at the Table: Agentic AI promises to close the chip design productivity gap, but the explosion of autonomous workloads is exposing fundamental limitations in how EDA data is stored, accessed, secured, and managed. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss this at the 2026 Design Automation Conference with Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at Cadence; Simon Rance, general manager, IP and Data Management Business at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI and Solido at Siemens EDA; Ramesh Narayanaswamy, scientist at Synopsys; and Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. What follows are excerpts of that discussion.

L-R: Cadence’s Alpert; Keysight EDA’s Rance; Siemens EDA’s Balasubramanian; Synopsys’ Narayanaswamy; IC Manage’s Drako.
SE: What are the biggest challenges your customers are dealing with for implementing AI in EDA data management?
Drako: The biggest problem facing large customers with globally distributed design systems is continuing to scale to larger, more complicated designs and to reuse IP. Right now, designs are a giant assembly of IP components that need to be assembled, verified, and put together. With AI coming into the equation, those customers want clean databases that the AI can use. They want easy access for the AI to get to that IP, leverage it, and manage the complexity the AI introduces in running more jobs faster. That puts a bigger load on the design management system and the distribution of that data.
Alpert: There’s a huge productivity gap, so they need AI. It’s not like, ‘Oh, it would be nice, so we’re more productive.’ They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing,  even though EDA always improves year over year. Hopefully agentic AI will narrow the gap. In terms of deploying it, part of the biggest challenge is that there’s so much noise. There are so many options — internal/ external models, startups. How do they figure out what to do to make a production-worthy AI flow? That’s probably a real challenge for them.
Balasubramanian: What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff, both in terms of terms and nomenclature and what people think they can do and cannot do with AI. In the last couple of years, top customers have at least figured out what to do and what not to do at a high level, but the key challenge I see is that many new factors are coming into play. What they’re worried about right now is the quality they’re seeing. They want to have a deterministic flow. They also want to make sure that they are not overkilling in terms of their token budgets and compute infrastructure to get those same answers fast — correct answers. So there’s quite a bit of nuance in how they’re deploying, and it’s really based on where they are focusing and what problem they’re solving. And they are getting to a point where they know what to solve. It’s not like this push-button flow for the entire problem, where you push a button and say I want a chip for this case. They are becoming more realistic. And another point is there are so many variables. Every customer wants to do everything, but then they get stuck in this loophole about what is the right thing to do.
Narayanaswamy: In dealing with customers, we see they’re looking to close the productivity gap. There are all these magic numbers, like we are 2× short of the number of designers people want for all these new design starts people want. On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors of issues. One is, ‘Where the heck is my data going?’ Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not. But somebody needs to govern that. Or even, ‘Under what contract are you handing that to an LLM?’
Drako: An LLM might go and use something that you didn’t know it used.
Narayanaswamy: If you don’t have an enterprise account with Anthropic and you don’t click the right button, everything you’re doing is there, and Anthropic will train with what they want. So the governance is one. The second is the internal things we build out of this. So you have agentic memory. That sounds good. It helps the flow, but what did you stick in it? And when I am transitioning from, say, when this chip is done, or this block is done, to the next design, what do I carry forward? Historically, we haven’t saved reproducible stuff. But now, there’s a whole new set of things. And the third thing is that models are, in some ways, horrible at dealing with the volume of data. You say I have a waveform database. The model is smart enough to take that waveform database and turn it into text. But that waveform database was like a terabyte of stuff, and you just spent how many tokens going there? You need to provide something where the model can query what it needs or the abstraction it needs. I’ve even seen where, if you give a model enough time, it starts writing a little MCP server. It goes and finds the API from somewhere. So it’s doing all these sub-optimal things, and I don’t think our customers can afford this stuff anymore at scale. Those are things we are looking to solve.
Rance: Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years now, and they’re realizing they’re sitting on a treasure trove of data to leverage for AI. But the challenges that they’re finding are that data is all over the place. What’s the quality of that data? How can we trust that data? And then, how can we govern and secure that data so it doesn’t get released to an LLM, flawed, or to the wrong people? Data management has been seen as a necessity, but it’s just about managing the data. Now it’s, ‘How do you help us find that data, organize it, secure it, and control it so our AI isn’t leaking any of our IP?’ And, ‘How can AI can leverage that and help with better reuse of IP?’ That’s been a challenge for 20 years or so. Solutions like IC Manage, ours, Perforce, and others help with IP reuse, but how it’s packaged and how reusable it is are always a challenge. In the AI era, there’s a lot more automation that can be wrapped around that to help with real IP reuse, but it comes back to those foundational pillars that our customers are seeing in that challenge — quality, trust, and how we cover and trace it.
SE: Scaling was mentioned right off the bat. What does this mean for EDA data management today?
Drako: An engineering project to design a chip may be 10 engineers, 100 engineers, or 1,000 engineers. But what we want, to overcome the productivity issues that everyone’s bringing up, is to use agents to augment those engineers. So maybe have those engineers, instead of operating in 10 workspaces in one workspace each, have 10 or 20 agents that each of them is directing. They get parallelism with all these agents doing work, and they’re more like the director of the orchestra, and so their productivity goes up. To do that, those agents need workspaces. They’re checking stuff out of the version control system or out of the design management system, they’re doing work on it, and then they’re checking it back in, and so you’ve just 10× or 20×’d the load on your design management system, your network file system (NFS), and you’ve 10× or 20×’d the number of licenses you need to buy from Cadence or Siemens or Synopsys or Keysight, or whoever, because you know that that much more is going on. So there’s a scaling issue. We focused on scaling the design management piece, which we’ve always been very strong at. But if you go and say, I’ve got 1,000 engineers, which used to have 1,000 workspaces that you’re managing and updating on an hourly basis, now I’ve got 25,000. The scaling problem is quite large, so that’s one aspect. Then we’ve done a lot of work on the NFS component. NFS is a great solution, but everything has to go over the network. It’s very inefficient. It’s a very chatty protocol, so it’s slow. That means all our customers are constantly fighting speed issues with the file system and the servers. When you want to launch a regression run, and it’s going to launch at 10 p.m. when everybody’s out, but it’s going to launch on 5,000 servers, you’ve got to get all 5,000 servers to have the same data so that you can run all those regression tests. That’s a huge load on the file systems. We had one customer who would launch the regressions every night, and the elevator would stop running because they’d somehow hooked the elevator into the local network, so nobody could leave. So we introduced what is essentially an NFS booster to help with that problem. And then you’ve also got scaling of CAD. If you think about it, there’s a small organization of CAD and IT guys supporting 100 or 1000 engineers. Now they’ve got to support 100,000 engineers plus 10,000 agents, who are also trying to use that same infrastructure to get work done.
Narayanaswamy: An interesting side of scaling the business is also velocity. We were running some experiments, and somebody said, “Look, we run these 20 epochs, but it’s actually over 20 nightly runs. Suddenly, those 20 epochs are happening in 8 hours. So you grab the LSF queue, and your agent is hanging on to it. So the bursty workload is one thing. Predictability is another.
Drako: One of the things customers are very concerned about, and is a big focus, is security. Inside of [our technology], there are a lot of security components to limit access, often for government contracts, often for locations in other countries where they don’t want them to have full access to everything in the design. There are lots of very practical reasons that aren’t really obvious when you just think about it, and so all of those security components, security restrictions, or security controls are going to be critical in the AI execution as well because the AI can get a little rambunctious and actually kind of start creating things like you mentioned and try to get to things. We’ve seen a bunch of stories in the press about AI going rogue and digging into places it shouldn’t. With those security issues, oftentimes there’s security by obscurity, or mediocre security constraints, or people haven’t thought through the security a whole lot. There’s going to be a lot more in the data management world around security with AI in the game, because AI doesn’t necessarily have the same conscience that an employee might, and it isn’t bound by the same laws.
Narayanaswamy: That’s why we’re going around doing secure sandboxes. The more conscious customer is really saying, ‘There’s an LLM call. I need to know what access that sub-agent is going to have.’ It needs to be bounded. Most customers have gotten smarter. They used to do the air gap themselves.
Balasubramanian: One customer said, ‘Every prompt is an IP that I’m giving away. If I’m trying to say, ‘Do this in a way that does this,’ that’s the way I’m actually designing or doing something. I’m actually giving advice, so we really are planning to go for air-gapped on-prem.’ I would say everyone is thinking about it right now.
Alpert: That trend’s reversing now. A year and a half ago, all customers were saying, ‘Oh yeah, only air-gapped on-prem. We need to use open-source models.’ But frontier models like Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini have gotten so good that people don’t want to sacrifice quality. They’re figuring out how they can use these and connect with them. I’d say more customers are on that side of the fence now, but maybe they’re also making special deals where they can host it themselves.
Drako: Customers are figuring it out. Because it’s all new, there’s a big strategy question: ‘Do I go and invest in my own AI models and train them on my designs?’ These are all LLMs, and they do very well when it’s language. If I’m looking at Verilog, they’ll do well. If I’m looking at a waveform file, they don’t understand it, so they convert it to text. If I’m looking at layout, they don’t understand it. They’ve never been trained on it. They’ve never seen it, and it’s not words. There’s a big question of who’s going to create AI models that are trained on it and understand it. Is that going to be the EDA companies, or the Nvidias and AMDs who are going to go do that? They don’t know right now. Everybody’s trying to figure it out.
Rance: We’re seeing a bit of a hybrid of that, where we’re training our own models, but then we’re creating the infrastructure to provide to them. So they can add and create their own models in conjunction with that, and get a lot more value when they combine our EDA tools with the models and the data. Then they’re using the environment to train and create their surrogate models, put that into the workflow, and build trust between the two. ‘This is what it’s doing. It’s contained to that, secured. We don’t have to worry about it going rogue.’ They’re doing it in small phases and rolling it out, but they’re creating agentic workflows that are very tightly constrained right now to prevent leakage.
Narayanaswamy: In terms of the modeling, Chuck makes an important point. When you need reasoning, if you don’t use a frontier model, you may be applying the wrong tool. But for the more domain-specific stuff, there’s this hybrid where you could have sub-domain models, even some very specialized things. Models seem terrible at things like assertions, which are very specialized temporal assertions that reason over time. And you could say, ‘Let’s have a model that is quite good at assertions — but for reasoning.’ That is the tension. Maybe folks like Anthropic need to come to the table and provide a level of trust. It’s a ‘trust me’ business with all of them. Something has to change there.
Alpert: When it comes to training models, the problem with that is like, ‘Okay, let me pick a model to train. It’s probably open-source, which means it’s probably already behind the frontier models. Now I’m going to work on that for three to four months and deploy it to the customer. But now it’s probably a year behind because some new model will come out. That means the training we’ve done has to be good enough to pass. That’s a tough, tough game, and it’s a cat-and-mouse game. It’s like, ‘I train on this model, but now I have to retrain on some new model.’ The danger is that the frontier models will just obliterate what we’ve trained. That’s happened before. Will it continue to happen? I don’t know. Maybe they’re stuck in a place. Then three months from now, it’s like, ‘Oh, there’s a model that’s pretty good at that and understands it.’
Balasubramanian: The frontier models are getting better, but one thing they still lack is enterprise data. They just don’t have access to it. On the front-end side, they can probably get away with it, but not on the RTL generation side.
Drako: They don’t need it. There’s enough RTL code out there publicly that they can get. They can do it, but there are not a whole lot of layouts in the public world.
Alpert: Here’s where I’ll disagree. We can now do skills. We can now give expertise to LLMs, so you could say a lot of people who do place-and-route actually never look at it. They’re just command-line junkies, and they get reports and the like.
Drako: That’s if you’re using the tool. But that’s the command-line interface, the log files, the human interface. The LLM can plug in and do what the human did on the tool. But if you actually want to get AI in the tool, and the results aren’t a log file, you want to look at the layout and say, ‘Oh, that’s not the layout I want.’
Alpert: It’s one thing to say we’re trying to make humans more productive, so we can now automate the job they did with the stuff with the command line. What you’re saying is that you think we could reach a higher level of PPA.
Drako: You’ve just got to differentiate those two piles.
Alpert: So as we’ve been saying about closing the design productivity gap, that’s not needed. You don’t need trained models. But if you want to reach that next level, then now it’s time for some real creativity. What’s going to be really interesting is how we as an industry, for example, write a new place-and-route tool that’s truly agentic, image-based, and all that.
Drako: It will eventually happen. It’s inevitable.
Alpert: But quantum computing is a matter of time, and I’ve been hearing about it for 30 years. I’ll be retired by the time it comes out.
SE: Quantum is 5 to 10 years out.
Alpert: Quantum might be available today, but when is more than 1% of semiconductor revenue going to go to quantum? That’s my bar. Like, is that 5 years, 10 years, 20 years? I don’t know.
